title: Original BLITZ: two mirrored four-bar collectors
construction: Dual four-bars; X44 deployment at 79.37:1; separate X60 roller drives.
team_stated_reason: Collect sideways while passing; collapse under impacts.
engineering_analysis: This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.
recommended_validation: Compare opposite-side sweep paths against turning a single-intake robot, including one damaged linkage and time to replace it.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: Original BLITZ: serpentine inventory and passing
construction: Serpentine conveyor, two X60 feeder motors, three X60 shooter motors; variable hood.
team_stated_reason: Use the alliance zone as storage for a passing-centered role.
engineering_analysis: The low-storage concept treats the field as an external buffer. Its success requires the alliance to recover that buffered fuel at the right time and place. Passing capacity and scoring capacity are different services even when the same launcher performs both. A continuous serpentine can constrain fuel well but adds contact length, curved transitions and friction; a well-controlled ball path may still be unable to supply enough mass flow. This original brief must be read alongside the later rebuild account: a design rationale is evidence of a hypothesis, not evidence that the hypothesis met the team’s competitive targets.
recommended_validation: Measure fuel moved to a recoverable location, residual path inventory, and scoring available after the passer returns; vary partner collection quality.
limitations: The brief describes a 25-fuel/s feed capability; the later account reports inadequate overall performance. Do not treat that number as an independently demonstrated match average.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: RE-BLITZ: strengthened slapdown
construction: Four-bar replaced by slapdown; 0.6-inch plates; #35 deployment chain; powered bottom roller.
team_stated_reason: Strength, service access and reliable full-speed acquisition.
engineering_analysis: A single pivot simplifies the force path: an exposed roller loads its arms, pivot and hard stop without several moving links sharing the impact. That does not make it automatically more impact tolerant. The stronger arm and larger deployment chain need a corresponding chassis attachment and a stop that can react a collision without loading the gearbox teeth. Powering the lower contact also matters at the bumper transition: fuel can otherwise be caught between a moving upper roller and a stationary surface while the robot continues advancing. Plate stiffness and ball transport are separate improvements and should be tested separately.
recommended_validation: Test a wall hit and an oblique corner hit, then remeasure roller alignment and deployment current; test full-speed pickup of worn fuel.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: RE-BLITZ: preserve width through the floor and tower
construction: Ten inclined floor rollers; four-X60 feeder; Teflon backing; enlarged four-wide path.
team_stated_reason: Remove restrictions between hopper and launcher.
engineering_analysis: Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Inclination and backing determine the normal force and the direction in which fuel escapes when multiple balls arrive together. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.
recommended_validation: Log feeder current, wheel speed and scored output through a full hopper; repeat with 5, 15 and 30 fuel and with deliberate asymmetric loading.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: RE-BLITZ: drum, hood rollers and flywheel recovery
construction: Four-inch drum, 1.5-inch hood rollers, overdriven flywheel; team reports >30 fuel/s and a 34 maximum.
team_stated_reason: High discharge rate with manageable shooter recovery.
engineering_analysis: A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.
recommended_validation: Measure per-lane velocity and accuracy before and after a long volley; log loaded battery voltage and recovery between successive shots.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: RE-BLITZ: expansion actuated by the intake
construction: Intake-driven hopper expansion; smooth internal sheet-metal joints; deployed one-way catchers.
team_stated_reason: Store useful inventory and feed it back toward the shooter.
engineering_analysis: The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.
recommended_validation: Interrupt deployment halfway with a full hopper; test reverse motion, ball trapping at panel overlaps, trench travel and final-fuel evacuation.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: RE-BLITZ: mechanism readiness and fallback operation
construction: Shot gates, vision-based targeting, CANrange preload sensing and fixed-position manual fallbacks.
team_stated_reason: Coordinate feeding with the actual launch state.
engineering_analysis: A high mechanical ceiling can be lost to premature feed. The feeder must distinguish an intentional firing pause from a jam, an empty hopper and a shooter that has not recovered. Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.
recommended_validation: Disable one camera, introduce an empty-hopper sensor error and force a heading correction mid-volley; check the operator can recover predictably.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: BEARRICADE: collector evolution and impact reinforcement
construction: Three rollers; dead-axle polycarbonate tubes; later metal stub-axle reinforcement.
team_stated_reason: Remove pickup dead zones and improve impact survival.
engineering_analysis: A compliant tube may survive bending while its end attachment fails. That makes the stub axle, bearing retention and local side-plate load path as important as the roller material. A lower transition roller closes the region where a single upper roller can push fuel rather than capture it. More contact points can improve acquisition, but they also add belt drag and opportunities for a ball to be over-compressed. The relevant question is whether the ball experiences a continuous forward velocity through the bumper transition, including when the robot is moving and the hopper is already full.
recommended_validation: Film pickup from the side at maximum approach speed; inspect stub-axle displacement after repeated oblique hits.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: BEARRICADE: linked hopper and capacity states
construction: Collector-linked sliding walls; net; reported 60 fuel under trench and 75–80 over bump.
team_stated_reason: Increase useful storage without losing the travel state.
engineering_analysis: These capacity figures describe different operating envelopes, not one universally available volume. A net can retain the top layer while allowing a changing envelope, but it adds elastic forces and can push fuel into the throat or against a wall. Sliding walls need enough overlap to remain guided under a side load without creating an inward shelf. Coupling deployment to the collector saves an actuator and synchronizes the opening, but also couples hopper faults to pickup. A good borrowed implementation preserves service access and allows the robot to recover when only one side deploys correctly.
recommended_validation: Measure retained and feedable capacity after loaded bump travel, then test deployment with a damaged slide or displaced net.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: BEARRICADE: why the belt bed became rollers
construction: Belt bed abandoned; ten 1.25-inch rollers, successive 21:20 speed steps, two X44s.
team_stated_reason: Belt tension and ball motion were limiting the early design.
engineering_analysis: A belt bed pulls continuously on its support shafts; the tension required to transmit power can bend those shafts even before fuel loading is considered. A roller floor moves that challenge into shaft spacing, surface grip and transmission design. Incrementally faster rollers can stretch spacing between balls, but only if the fuel actually follows the surface and does not simply slip. Agitation is not automatically helpful: repeated upward kicks can keep a ball from settling into the receiving contact. This is why a rate test must observe the inlet to the superstructure, not only the speed of the floor.
recommended_validation: Measure time to empty under several fill levels, compare stepped speeds against equal speeds, and count time balls spend recirculating at the inlet.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: BEARRICADE: integrated S-path and two-lane drum
construction: Four-inch drum; printed backing; hood range −10° to 60°; triple-lane prototype became dual.
team_stated_reason: Match launch capacity to indexing and preserve packaging.
engineering_analysis: Reducing lane count can improve the robot if the extra lane forces a worse feeder, more current or a larger structure. The S-shaped path is an integration choice, not a universal superiority claim over a J-shaped route. Negative launch angles create a specific close-to-hub shot envelope; they need geometric clearance and empirical tuning, especially where the robot is braced against a field element. Integrating shooter and tower plates can remove redundant material and align contact surfaces, while increasing the consequence of damage to that shared structure. The same binder also shows a turret concept; that image alone does not prove it competed.
recommended_validation: Test near-hub reverse shots and far shots at depleted battery; inspect integrated plate deflection while the feeder is fully loaded.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: BEARRICADE: delete the low-value climb
construction: The team rejected a six-pound, ten-point climbing package that occupied hopper space.
team_stated_reason: Fuel contribution outweighed the mechanism’s opportunity cost.
engineering_analysis: This is direct team evidence for treating climb as a low-priority 2026 architecture choice. Its cost is larger than its actuator and hook: it can remove storage, require alignment practice, complicate wiring and consume testing that could improve fuel flow. A calculation that includes only seconds spent climbing misses those development and packaging costs. Conversely, a near-free existing device could have a different marginal cost. The agent should begin with the observed fuel-dominant game, then require a specific positive marginal case before adding climb. It should not recommend one merely because the manual awards points for it.
recommended_validation: Compare scored-fuel loss from displaced volume and lost testing time against the expected climb contribution in the intended event role.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DESPERATE MEASURES: linear collector as a controllable spring
construction: Double-layer polycarbonate rack; two 2-inch rollers; low-stator-current deployment.
team_stated_reason: Large acquisition area with passive impact retraction.
engineering_analysis: A backdrivable, current-limited rack can yield during a collision rather than make the gearbox a rigid stop. That behavior depends on friction, reduction, acceleration limits and the controller remaining enabled; it is not supplied by polycarbonate alone. Stacking a structural plate beside the rack allows the designer to distribute load without relying only on gear teeth. A paired-roller collector should preserve positive contact as fuel crosses the bumper. The matching chassis and slide must react lateral hits, because a low-current motor primarily helps the axial direction.
recommended_validation: Measure peak rack load during frontal and sideways impacts; check tooth engagement and deployment after the test.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DESPERATE MEASURES: active floor and inventory policy
construction: 1.5-inch powered floor rollers; net; CANrange minimum-inventory control while passing.
team_stated_reason: Keep fuel available for the next scoring shift.
engineering_analysis: Inventory sensing changes the job of a passer. Passing every available ball can improve the alliance pile but leave this robot empty when the shift turns. A minimum reserve is a control policy tied to how quickly the robot can refill, return and shoot. A distance sensor sees a local surface, not a perfect total count; a sloped or bridged pile can produce the same reading at very different usable inventories. The threshold needs validation under different pile shapes and while accelerating. Reserve logic should have an operator override when alliance strategy intentionally assigns all fuel elsewhere.
recommended_validation: Compare sensor reading with deliverable inventory for uneven fills and motion; measure reserve adequacy at the start of each shift.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DESPERATE MEASURES: constrained belts and collision sorting
construction: Two rubber-coated conveyors, printed carryways, vertical kicker, quarter-pipe feed.
team_stated_reason: Turn bulk fuel into a reliable stream.
engineering_analysis: The carryway controls the support beneath the belt so compression does not change with belt sag. The vertical kicker addresses a different failure: two balls arriving at the quarter-pipe entrance can lock each other before either is captured. That distinction matters when diagnosing a singulator. Increasing belt speed does not necessarily release an arch; changing relative contact directions or reversing one element can. The quarter-pipe must preserve contact through the bend and deliver fuel at an appropriate velocity to the turret. A compact throat earns hopper space only if it remains serviceable and can clear a hard jam.
recommended_validation: Feed deliberately paired balls and partially collapsed fuel; log current signatures before and after reversal and inspect carryway wear.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DESPERATE MEASURES: compact turret and continuous hood
construction: Eight-inch bearing; ±185° turret; 4-inch Fairlane wheel; separate backspin kicker; variable hood.
team_stated_reason: Score and pass across a broad envelope.
engineering_analysis: The bearing and base plate must keep the launch contact aligned while the chassis accelerates and balls enter the shooter. Independent back contact permits spin tuning without changing the main wheel, but also introduces another speed and recovery condition. A range slightly greater than one turn reduces the frequency of an unwind; it does not create unlimited rotation. The cable chain must survive the worst combined hood and turret state. For a recommendation, the compact swept envelope and the singulator’s feed location are as important as the shooter’s wheel diameter.
recommended_validation: Map accuracy over turret angle and hood angle, including near both cable limits and under representative chassis acceleration.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DESPERATE TIMES to DESPERATE MEASURES
construction: Original hopperless four-to-two-to-one path replaced; turret reused; Orbit 1690 explicitly credited.
team_stated_reason: Original throughput did not justify minimal storage.
engineering_analysis: This is a valuable negative result because it separates the concept from its execution. A narrowing conveyor can spread fuel longitudinally as it accelerates, yet still fail to maintain sufficient launch supply. Without a hopper, every interruption in acquisition becomes an interruption in scoring. Reusing the turret preserved calibrated software and known interfaces while the rest of the architecture changed. The proper historical record includes both machines and the transition; the later successful package should not be projected backward onto the initial competitions or treated as a season-long fixed architecture.
recommended_validation: For a rebuild, identify which calibrated interfaces can survive unchanged and which performance assumptions require new integrated testing.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: CYCLONE: collector and frame share the impact path
construction: Full-width linear collector; 1.125-inch rollers; load-spreading hubs and washers.
team_stated_reason: Acquire five columns and survive contact.
engineering_analysis: An exposed roller’s compliance must be paired with a force path into the chassis. A small washer can concentrate force and start a crack even if the main plate is otherwise flexible. Distributing that load across a hub or a larger washer reduces local pressure, but the joint must still allow the intended movement. The collector width also has an autonomous geometry consequence: it changes which fuel columns can be reached without the chassis crossing a contested route. A width figure should be linked to the effective acquisition envelope rather than merely the distance between arms.
recommended_validation: Map acquisition success across the entire mouth with off-center hits, then repeat after controlled impact loading.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: CYCLONE: DYE-inspired rotor with independent feed
construction: 22-inch rotor; eight-fuel ring; separate rotation/feed drives; reported 18-fuel/s feed.
team_stated_reason: Maintain bulk-to-single-stream flow in a compact package.
engineering_analysis: A rotor is not just a rotating bucket. Its moving boundary, internal feed contact and exit geometry jointly determine whether fuel circulates, enters the ring, or jams. Independent feed drive lets the team tune the launch supply without requiring the whole bulk pile to turn at that speed. A lower-profile center obstruction improves the area through which fuel can enter; reversing must not turn a hook or seam into a trap. A theoretical ring count multiplied by rotation rate is only an upper bound: pockets must actually fill and discharge.
recommended_validation: Measure pocket occupancy and output variability at full, half and nearly empty loads; test reversing a deliberately bridged inlet.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: CYCLONE: floating hood, preload and turret support
construction: Compact turret; floating hood; constant-force spring; through-bore sensing; powered hood rollers.
team_stated_reason: Reduce backlash and preserve storage volume.
engineering_analysis: Spring preload can keep a reduction loaded against one tooth flank, reducing reversal uncertainty, but adds a torque that the motor must overcome in the opposite direction. Measuring the output rather than only the motor helps detect residual compliance between gearbox and hood. The feed path and turret bearing need common structural alignment; a compact height is valuable only if it does not permit the hood to deflect enough to change the exit angle. Powered hood rollers alter the spin/contact state, so their ratio belongs in the shot calibration rather than being treated as passive guidance.
recommended_validation: Measure hood angle repeatability from both approach directions and at several turret headings; compare loaded and unloaded structure.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: CYCLONE: moving-shot compensation and variable feed
construction: Gyro latency compensation, empirical flight time and variable rotor speed are documented.
team_stated_reason: Maintain accurate mobile firing and stable throughput.
engineering_analysis: A turret can cancel chassis heading only if the controller uses the correct observation time and the actual release state. A latency error grows with angular velocity and can look like a mechanical aiming bias. Rotor speed also changes shot timing and inlet loading; a firing command is not the same as a ball leaving the hood. The mechanical and control record should include this delay and its variation. Slowing the feed may improve delivered score if it reduces wheel droop or keeps the exit state within tolerance.
recommended_validation: Time-stamp vision, gyro, turret position, feeder transitions and ball release; compare miss direction against angular and translational velocity.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: 3467: redundant rack support and expanding walls
construction: Double polycarbonate rack plates; powered and idler pinions; walls move with intake.
team_stated_reason: Impact tolerance, tooth engagement and more storage.
engineering_analysis: Supporting a rack at more than one point reduces its tendency to peel away from the drive pinion under load. Two rack plates can distribute stress, but only if their tooth timing and guidance are aligned; otherwise they can fight each other. Moving the walls with the collector creates agitation as well as extra volume. Agitation may improve flow near the floor but can also throw a top layer out unless the lid and wall overlap control it. A side load remains a separate case from a frontal collapse.
recommended_validation: Test rack deflection, skipping and skew with a side hit; observe fuel near moving wall seams during repeated deploy/retract cycles.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: 3467: active centering into two launch streams
construction: Ten floor rollers; powered stacked-belt side wedges; central divider; live-axle tower roller.
team_stated_reason: Center fuel while limiting tower oscillation.
engineering_analysis: Active side contact can rotate or translate fuel away from a bottleneck rather than relying on gravity against a fixed wall. Its surface direction has to agree with the desired stream; excessive inward force can create an arch at the divider. The live-axle tower roller is a structural answer to rapidly changing multi-ball loads, reducing a source of compression variation. The useful comparison is not simply belts versus rollers: it is whether the particular contact geometry establishes two repeatable, supplied paths through the entire range of hopper fill.
recommended_validation: Feed off-center piles, log each stream separately, and compare tower deflection under single-ball and paired-ball arrivals.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: 3467: two independent launchers and stored energy
construction: Two launchers; four 3-inch 45A wheels per launcher with inertia kits; adjustable hood.
team_stated_reason: High rate with controllable exit conditions.
engineering_analysis: Independent launch drives can compensate for asymmetric supply, but increase the number of conditions that must be measured. Added inertia can reduce transient speed droop while consuming mass and spin-up time. A soft wheel increases compliance and contact duration, but changes compression as it wears or heats. Hood range should be translated into a validated scoring and passing envelope, rather than assuming every geometric angle produces a useful trajectory. The desired test is a full stream of representative fuel, not a single ideal ball launched repeatedly.
recommended_validation: Compare both streams’ exit speed distributions and accuracy through a long volley, at fresh and worn surface conditions.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: 3467: camera structure and predictive trench ducking
construction: Braced camera towers; measured shot gates; future-pose hood retraction for trench entry.
team_stated_reason: Preserve localization and avoid hood collisions.
engineering_analysis: Camera vibration produces an apparent pose error even if the vision algorithm is otherwise correct. Bracing the mount to the shooter can stiffen it, but also transmits shooter vibration; the net effect should be measured. Trench protection is a dynamic clearance problem: retracting at the boundary is too late when the mechanism takes time to move. The lookahead should include speed, control delay, deceleration and an uncertainty margin, with a safe fallback if localization becomes invalid. This is a control requirement created by the mechanism’s envelope.
recommended_validation: Run approach tests at several speeds and headings with degraded pose data; verify the hood clears before the physical entry plane.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR original: linear collection and linked hopper
construction: Rack deployment, multiple powered rollers, pin-slot hopper extension.
team_stated_reason: Compact stow and broad acquisition.
engineering_analysis: The intake and expanding wall are physically linked, so their travel, friction and alignment cannot be optimized independently. A pin-slot joint can accommodate different trajectories but may create a high local pressure at the end of travel. A multirotor pickup needs enough overlap to avoid an uncontrolled interval as fuel crosses the bumper. If the linkage binds, commanding more motor torque can damage the rack before solving the wall alignment. The architecture should retain a way to inspect and replace the joint without disassembling the whole fuel path.
recommended_validation: Cycle the linkage under hopper side loading and inspect slot wear; test an interrupted deployment and recovery.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR original: serpentine and turret feed
construction: Belt serpentine; curved backing replaces interfering upper wheels; 400° turret.
team_stated_reason: Compact routing with controlled feed and independent aim.
engineering_analysis: Removing a wheel can improve a mechanism when the wheel occupies the same space needed by another moving assembly. Curved backing trades active contact for sliding contact and must keep fuel captured through the bend. The turret’s rotation range is a cable-management specification as much as an aiming specification. The original design and its later replacement are separate records: a successful collection system does not prove the single-stream scorer met the team’s later competitive needs. Prototype targets must remain labeled targets even when the surrounding prose sounds confident.
recommended_validation: Sweep the full turret range while feeding deliberately varied fuel, and compare useful output with the original target under realistic voltage.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: repair the collision path
construction: Single-pivot intake; higher round bash bar; extra motor-plate bracing; passive lower bar.
team_stated_reason: Stop bar deflection from stalling rollers; save power and weight.
engineering_analysis: A bash bar can become the failure if it bends into the very roller it protects. Moving the reaction member above the rotating contact changes that failure geometry. Reverting a powered element to a passive surface is an important counterexample to the rule that more powered contacts always help: the added drive may cost current without improving capture in the tested geometry. This result should not be transferred blindly to another bumper gap or approach speed. It supports testing the actual bottleneck and force path before adding a motor.
recommended_validation: Measure bar-to-roller clearance after impact; compare capture probability and current with powered and passive lower contact.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: net, trench access and electrical relocation
construction: Net-topped storage; bumper-mounted panels; electrical panel flipped upward.
team_stated_reason: Retain fuel, use trench routes and protect electronics.
engineering_analysis: A bumper-mounted wall can simplify robot mass allocation but introduces a service interface: removing or shifting the bumper can change hopper alignment and expose a gap. The net adds a travel envelope that depends on fuel loading and deformation. Flipping the electrical panel exchanges one exposure for another, so the skid plate, drainage and access plan must be considered with the new layout. The correct capacity test measures fuel retained after the actual route and then delivered to the shooter, rather than the empty CAD volume.
recommended_validation: Remove and reinstall bumpers repeatedly, inspect wall alignment, then run full-load trench and bump routes followed by complete discharge.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: single-stream turret to four-wide drum
construction: Four-wide transfer; mixed-diameter rollers; three X60 shooter drives and two feeder drives.
team_stated_reason: Original single stream was too slow for the intended competition level.
engineering_analysis: The rebuild changes both the launcher and the supply path. Wider discharge without wider feeding would preserve the original restriction. Gradually accelerating fuel can reduce crowding before launch, but it must preserve contact and avoid forcing balls against a stationary roof. The strategic claim is specific to this team’s execution and operating conditions; it does not invalidate compact turrets that achieve a different combination of capacity, sustained firing and maneuverability. Preserve the original development and the district-to-DCMP transition so a recommendation can learn from the pivot rather than only its final appearance.
recommended_validation: Compare complete cycle score against the original under the same fuel supply, defense and active-window timing.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: DOWNPOUR: proposed telescope and later compact hooks
construction: Original telescope did not compete at districts; later pivoting hooks replaced it.
team_stated_reason: Weight, space and scoring priorities displaced the initial climb.
engineering_analysis: The presence of a climber CAD image in an early binder is not proof it was installed or used. The later brief supplies a useful version boundary by explicitly saying the earlier mechanism did not compete. The new hook package should be recorded as a compact capability, not evidence that climbing became strategically central. In a fuel-dominant game, retain the opportunity cost in storage, mechanism power, alignment and testing. A low-mass hook can still be a poor choice if it blocks a valuable fuel route.
recommended_validation: Audit actual installation and match use separately from prototype drawings; calculate lost usable fuel volume before selecting a climbing package.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

title: 971 2022: a deliberate West Coast drive simplicity choice
construction: Six Colson-wheel West Coast drive; two dual-Falcon gearboxes; 8:70 gearbox tooth ratio.
team_stated_reason: Robustness, low maintenance and short-distance acceleration.
engineering_analysis: A differential drive sacrifices direct sideways motion while reducing the number of independent drive and steering mechanisms. That trade can fit a robot whose turret provides aiming independence and whose collectors support acquisition from opposite sides. Wheel choice affects maintenance and turning losses as well as traction. The team’s post-COVID experience constraint is part of this architecture decision: the most sophisticated available module is not automatically the strongest choice when integration and practice capacity differ. Preserve the resource assumption rather than presenting a universal drivetrain ranking.

title: 971 2022: center and guide cargo rather than only gripping harder
construction: Flex-wheel prototype became mecanum-centered pickup with compliant chain/arm geometry and extra upper guides.
team_stated_reason: Use known intake behavior and improve transfer support.

Mecanum contact supplies centering while the compliant arm accommodates shape and pressure variation. Additional upper rollers address the transition after the initial capture, where a ball can lose support or arrive at the receiver at an uncontrolled height. title: 971 2022: flippy arms combine retention and release
construction: Spring-loaded paired transfer arms; one-way-bearing action opens them when rollers reverse.
team_stated_reason: Hold cargo in the catapult, then release it for firing.
engineering_analysis: The transfer mechanism serves as a timed constraint on the projectile. It must hold the cargo through turret alignment but stop exerting an unwanted force at release. Coupling reversal to opening reduces an actuator but creates a mechanical timing relationship that software must understand. Spring force and ball compression affect both retention and release delay. If the catapult controller assumes the ball is free before the arms actually clear, a perfectly tracked motor trajectory can still produce a poor shot.

title: 971 2022: a controlled catapult instead of a flywheel
construction: Light carbon catapult, two Falcons, 7:99 tooth ratio and model-predictive launch control.
team_stated_reason: Team prototypes favored tolerance to cargo pressure and surface-friction variation.
engineering_analysis: A motor-driven catapult sets the projectile’s velocity through the motion of a supporting arm rather than relying primarily on slip against a high-speed wheel. That can reduce one source of friction sensitivity while introducing trajectory tracking, release timing and structural stiffness requirements. A lighter arm spends less energy accelerating itself and leaves more actuator authority for the cargo. The controller needs the correct state at release, not merely a final position, because angle and velocity together determine the shot. This is a specific tested alternative, not a claim that catapults universally beat flywheels.

title: 971 2022: turret structure must also react climbing loads
construction: Turret carries catapult and climber; paired bearing support; climber revisions progress toward a spring-extended high-bar package.
team_stated_reason: Support firing and hanging loads with compact packaging.
engineering_analysis: A bearing sized only for smooth aiming may be inadequate once the suspended robot applies an overturning moment through the turret. Two support locations can define a load path for that moment while maintaining axis alignment. Shared structure saves space but couples the climber’s strength requirements to the shooter’s pointing stiffness. title: AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances
construction: 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.
team_stated_reason: Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.
engineering_analysis: Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.

title: AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis
construction: Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.
engineering_analysis: Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.
recommended_validation: Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.
limitations: Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.

title: AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff
construction: Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.
team_stated_reason: Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.
engineering_analysis: A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.
recommended_validation: Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.

title: AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder
construction: Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.
team_stated_reason: Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.
engineering_analysis: The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.
recommended_validation: Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers
construction: Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.
team_stated_reason: Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.
engineering_analysis: A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.
recommended_validation: Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: AURELIA: reuse the shoulder and reposition the cage
construction: Powered cage capture, passive latches, sliding support and shoulder-driven lifting; algae intake supplies support.
team_stated_reason: Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.
engineering_analysis: A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”

title: SPECTRE: base and module revision at Championship
construction: District Mk4i modules changed to prototype Mk5 at Worlds; ballast placement also changed.

A wide tread and different enclosure can alter friction, debris protection and maintenance. Retuning drive and autonomous behavior is part of the mechanical change: old acceleration and feedforward assumptions should not be carried over without measurements. title: SPECTRE: remote power at an integrated pivot
construction: Separate three-X60 shoulder and extension gearboxes; dead-axle pivot; two-stage cascade arm.
team_stated_reason: Fast motion with a low stowed center of gravity and serviceable arm.

The price is a more complicated transmission across the pivot and through the telescope. A coaxial extension drive must preserve tension and alignment over the shoulder’s range. A large shared pivot can support stiffness and removal, but its clamps and end plugs become critical load interfaces. Motor count alone does not explain speed: the arm’s inertia, reduction, current limits and acceleration profile determine whether it can move quickly without rocking the chassis.

title: SPECTRE: acquire, orient and score with one end mechanism
construction: Vertical and horizontal roller sets; four CANrange sensors; reversible front/back handoff and scoring.
team_stated_reason: Serve coral and algae tasks with the same manipulator.
engineering_analysis: Combining acquisition and scoring avoids a separate transfer interface, but makes the moving assembly larger and creates competing contact requirements. Coral has to be oriented differently for branches and L1; algae needs enough compliant pinch to stay captured during rapid motion. Multiple sensors can distinguish piece position and direction, provided their views remain reliable for both geometries. Front/back scoring reduces chassis rotation when the software chooses a sensible approach. The architecture should be assessed by complete cycle time and reach under defense, not by the number of available poses.

title: SPECTRE: moving climb carriage manages the hanging center
construction: Powered one-bar cage capture; carriage slides along arm; shoulder lifts; extension locks to bumper structure.
team_stated_reason: Balance under the chain while reusing the main arm.
engineering_analysis: The carriage is not just a convenient mount. Its translation changes where the cage pulls relative to the robot’s mass, allowing a controlled transition into suspension. The shoulder then supplies the lifting work and the arm lock supplies a post-match retention path. Those are separate functions and should be recorded separately. Reusing the arm reduces dedicated hardware but raises its required load and reliability. Any recommendation needs the actual cage contact, latch, shoulder and lock sequence rather than assuming that a strong scoring arm can safely substitute for a complete climber.

title: SPECTRE: automate approach choice and L1 placement

team_stated_reason: Remove repeated alignment work from the driver.
engineering_analysis: Choosing the nearest face or easiest orientation can save time, but the shortest geometric route is not always the least congested or the most valuable remaining target. L1 stacking creates an occupancy problem as well as a pose problem: a fixed placement height is insufficient once previous coral changes the landing surface. The driver still needs strategic control over task and side, with software handling repeatable motion. A mechanism recommendation should include the sensors, pose references and operator choices required to realize its cycle advantage.

title: UNDERTOW: short-cycle gearing and low mass placement
construction: 29.5-inch square base; low 3×1 frame; X2i modules geared about 13.2 ft/s free speed.
team_stated_reason: Favor acceleration and grip over long-run top speed.
engineering_analysis: For a short reef cycle, acceleration, braking and repeatable final alignment can matter more than a higher unloaded top speed. Lower gearing increases available wheel torque but does not guarantee traction; wheel compound, normal load and current limits still bound acceleration. A broad low base helps resist tipping while the elevator changes height, but occupies more traffic space. The useful comparison uses the actual route and raised mechanism state rather than a module specification on its own.

title: UNDERTOW: floating continuous rollers and four-bar deployment
construction: Foam/silicone continuous rollers, floating front plate, rubber-band dead-zone belts and four-bar deployment.
team_stated_reason: Admit longways coral and yield during collisions.
engineering_analysis: A continuous compliant surface can avoid the discrete kicks caused by spaced wheels, while a floating roller accommodates the changing cross-section presented by a tube approaching diagonally. Rubber bands bridge regions where neither main roller can maintain ownership. They also introduce wear, tracking and tension variables, so their role should be tested rather than treated as decorative assistance. The four-bar positions the deployed pickup without requiring its pivot at the very front of the chassis. Copy the contact geometry and trajectory together: substituting a single pivot can change both bumper clearance and handoff.
recommended_validation: Approach coral at a grid of angles, measure uninterrupted contact, and repeat after a wall impact and belt replacement.

title: UNDERTOW: flatten and index before handing off
construction: Eight compliant/star wheels; guide wedges, flattening yoke and beam breaks; separate steep station funnel.
team_stated_reason: Create a repeatable handoff from either source.
engineering_analysis: Ground and station pickup arrive with different velocities and orientations. A common indexer lets the end effector see a smaller set of input states, but the funnel and pickup must not feed incompatible positions. Wedges and a flattening wheel create deliberate constraints; if they constrain too many dimensions at once, the tube can wedge rather than align. Sensors should identify the indexed state before the receiver moves. The station funnel adds redundancy and autonomous options, so its value depends on how much extra envelope and mass it costs alongside floor acquisition.
recommended_validation: Compare handoff time and jam rate from both sources with skewed and bouncing arrivals; test the full state sequence after a missed detection.

title: UNDERTOW: fast continuous elevator
construction: Two-stage internal-belt lift; two X60s; welded support frame; team reports roughly 0.3-second full travel.
team_stated_reason: Reach scoring heights rapidly and maintain stiffness.
engineering_analysis: A fast travel number does not include settling, alignment or release. Internal belts protect the drive path but make access, tensioning and inspection more important. The support frame must react lateral inertia from the raised wrist as well as the elevator’s own acceleration. If the system reaches height quickly but sways outside the coral-placement tolerance, the useful cycle has not improved. A matched recommendation needs carriage mass, output stiffness, profile constraints and a maintenance plan rather than only belt width and motor count.
recommended_validation: Measure time until the coral tip enters and stays within scoring tolerance, not merely until the encoder reaches its height setpoint.

title: UNDERTOW: Flying V compliance and an L1 pass-through
construction: Wrist-mounted compliant coral roller, pipe-aligning Flying V, cam-controlled rear hoop and shared algae drive.
team_stated_reason: Fast branch placement with controlled piece handoff.
engineering_analysis: Mechanical alignment can absorb residual chassis error by guiding the end effector relative to the actual pipe. It must do so without pushing the tube into a trapped configuration or transmitting a large side load into the wrist. The movable hoop illustrates why the handoff and L1 scoring states differ: a stop that is necessary to receive coral can obstruct the intended exit. Sharing a motor between piece contacts reduces moving mass but couples their speed and torque requirements. The complete mechanism includes the cam state and sensing, not just the front roller.
recommended_validation: Map tolerated lateral and angular pipe error, test handoff against L1 pass-through, and repeat with a worn wheel and occupied nearby branches.

title: UNDERTOW: capture first, then winch the robot under the cage
construction: Powered roller claw, passive latch, gas-spring deployment and low-mounted ratcheting winch.
team_stated_reason: Acquire a cage quickly and retain suspension after disable.
engineering_analysis: Separating capture from lifting allows the capture wheels to optimize entry while the winch carries the robot load. The latch and cage reaction surfaces must take over reliably before the wheels stop providing traction. Remoting the winch lowers mass but lengthens the tension path and adds rope-routing concerns. A deep-climb recommendation should identify acquisition tolerance, how the cage rotates, where the chain ends relative to the robot’s center of mass, and the load path after power is removed.
recommended_validation: Test swinging-cage acquisition, transition from powered rollers to latch, and power-off retention with the actual rope routing.

title: MISS DAISY: orient on the floor and preserve collision compliance
construction: Sprung OTB rollers with ramps; later stronger front tube and round shafts.
team_stated_reason: Broad-orientation acquisition and impact survival.
engineering_analysis: Orienting the tube before lifting reduces the number of uncontrolled handoff states. A wide compliant roller captures early while ramps and passive contacts bias the tube toward the desired orientation. That can fail if a ramp starts lifting one end too soon. Structural damage also changes the ball path: a bent mounting tube can turn a nominally symmetric intake into a one-sided jam. Preserve the sequence of revisions, because a successful final contact geometry may rely on the preceding stiffness fix.
recommended_validation: Film diagonal approaches from both sides before and after impacts; measure ramp and roller alignment rather than judging symmetry by eye.

title: MISS DAISY: diagnose jams from observed contact
construction: Reduced compression, relocated support shaft, changed hard stops and redesigned ramp bends.
team_stated_reason: Slow-motion review identified different jams at successive events.
engineering_analysis: A jam is a geometric event, not merely insufficient motor power. A tube can press a belt into a support, climb at one end while the other end remains constrained, or stop a roller whose structure is bent. Each mode requires a different change. Moving the wheels forward changes both normal force and where the tube begins to rise. A useful agent should first ask which contacts stop moving and where the tube becomes over-constrained; recommending more torque without this observation can destroy the part that reveals the fault.
recommended_validation: Create a repeatable failed orientation, isolate the first contact that arrests motion, change one dimension and compare the failure frequency.

title: MISS DAISY: grip algae while allowing coral release
construction: Coral compression reduced to 0.375 inch; drive ratio revised; harder wheels and algae shields added.
team_stated_reason: Improve coral release, pulley durability and algae retention.
engineering_analysis: The two pieces demand conflicting grip behavior. Increasing compression can improve retention but make a tube difficult to release without disturbing the target. A harder wheel can resist wear yet reduce conformity and change normal force. A larger drive pulley may reduce tooth loading and skipping while changing speed and torque. Shields can prevent a soft ball from folding around the side plates, addressing a failure that motor current alone cannot solve. These are linked empirical tradeoffs, so the record should preserve both piece types and the tested release geometry.
recommended_validation: Measure coral release force and algae retention after representative wheel wear; inspect pulley teeth during repeated high-torque captures.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: MISS DAISY: rope geometry and structural stiffness evolved together
construction: Horizontal Dyneema spool inspired by 1678; continuous lift; later U-crossplate and rigid side support.
team_stated_reason: Solve rope slip, poor tension and elevator lateral play.
engineering_analysis: A lift can have accurate motor position while its carriage moves laterally because the structure and rope system are different error sources. Rope routing should keep each run aligned as winding radius changes; overlapping wraps change effective motion per motor turn. A stiff top crosspiece limits upright splay, while a triangulated or rigid support reacts side loading without relying only on adjustable rods. These revisions show why copying the final spool alone is insufficient. The recommendation needs the complete routing, tension system and support geometry.
recommended_validation: Track carriage height versus motor position and lateral tip error independently; inspect winding over repeated full strokes under load.
limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: MISS DAISY: shoulder and wrist serve different coordinates
construction: 45:1 shoulder with lantern gear; 21.4:1 wrist with about ±100° motion.
team_stated_reason: Move between robot sides and reorient coral without collisions.
engineering_analysis: The shoulder changes the end effector’s position and reach, while the wrist changes the piece orientation. Those motions need not be performed serially, but simultaneous movement requires a collision-aware path. A lantern gear can place the reduction close to the output and control backlash; its performance still depends on bearing alignment and tooth/pin wear. A dead-axle wrist offers a clear reaction path, but the cantilevered mass and cable routing contribute torque and deflection. The useful model is the coral’s swept volume, not only each joint’s independent limit.
recommended_validation: Generate and physically check the coral envelope during side swaps; measure output angle repeatability under reversing load.

title: MISS DAISY: passive harpoon over a wheeled grabber
construction: Levering climber; passive sprung harpoon; 675:1 reduction; steel gears replaced inadequate aluminum gears.
team_stated_reason: Similar capture performance with fewer vulnerable parts.
engineering_analysis: A high reduction can provide lifting torque, but it does not reduce the load carried by the final gear and support shaft. Material changes at that interface can therefore matter more than adding motor power. A passive hook can outperform powered acquisition when the robot’s approach already supplies sufficient engagement force and the cage geometry naturally directs the bar into the latch. That simplifies the controller while placing more importance on the approach envelope and retention geometry. Capture reliability should be assessed with swing and imperfect alignment, not only a stationary cage.

title: MISS DAISY: remove a dedicated algae intake that adds no useful capability
construction: A separate floor-algae collector was removed after prototype comparisons.
team_stated_reason: It did not outperform the end effector enough to justify complexity.
engineering_analysis: A subsystem can satisfy its own requirements and still be a poor robot-level choice. A dedicated collector may save a little positioning time while costing envelope, sensors, wiring, maintenance and driver decisions. If the primary end effector already serves the intended algae role, the marginal gain must exceed those costs. This is the right level for an architecture agent to reason: compare complete task contribution and reliability rather than rewarding more mechanisms. Keep the removed design in the history as an evaluated alternative, not as an installed feature of the final robot.

title: OPR 2025: floating capture and protected pivot drive
construction: 20-inch OTB intake; coaxial roller drive; synchronized pivot sides; floating upper roller.
team_stated_reason: Tolerant coral pickup with motors protected in the frame.
engineering_analysis: Coaxial power transmission lets a roller remain driven as the intake pivots without a long changing-center belt run. The floating contact accommodates an awkward tube orientation while the lower contact keeps it moving into the robot. Synchronizing both sides resists twist, but an impact can still concentrate load at the polycarbonate-to-aluminum joint. Large clamps distribute this force and retain the bearing as the plate flexes. Automatic retraction protects the collector only after the sensor has confirmed that the tube is safely inside.

title: OPR 2025: independent straightening drives and staged cradle sensing
construction: Independently driven straightener sides; current-triggered reversal; two-sensor cradle with anti-bounce step.
team_stated_reason: Align coral and recover jams before handoff.
engineering_analysis: Independent sides permit relative slip or reversal instead of forcing both ends of a tube forward at the same speed. Current sensing can identify resistance, but must distinguish a normal capture transient from a persistent jam. The cradle then changes the problem from continuous alignment to a discrete known handoff position. A stop lip and anti-bounce feature control longitudinal motion, while cutouts provide room for the receiving gripper. Excessively constraining the tube at the same time as the gripper closes can create a new jam, so the handoff sequence matters as much as the tray shape.

title: OPR 2025: reduce moving inertia without losing algae grip
construction: Formed-sheet arm replaced tubing; lighter geared gripper drive; remoted motor; velocity-matched coral ejection.
team_stated_reason: Reduce mass and pivot moment while keeping functional grip.
engineering_analysis: Removing mass far from the pivot reduces inertia more effectively than removing the same mass near the axis. A remoted motor achieves that while adding a transmission whose backlash and compliance must be controlled. Formed sheet can provide a stiff section with low mass if the flanges and joints react the actual loads. Matching ejection to chassis motion can reduce unwanted relative velocity at release, but requires consistent roller surface speed and piece position. It is a coordinated robot motion, not a passive property of the gripper.

title: OPR 2025: stiff internally belted elevator
construction: Two-stage continuous lift, internal 18-mm HTD belt, two X60s; reported about 0.6-second travel.
team_stated_reason: Fast motion with lateral stiffness and camera visibility.

title: Preacceleration, passive restraint and retrofit compression
construction: The interview describes a two-X44 intake at 2.5:1, passive carbon upper roller, roller-floor transmission described as 17:19, and a 3-inch steel drum driven by four X60s with powered hood rollers. A previously powered upper feed roller was made passive after jamming. Drum-region compression is reported as 3/8 inch and final roller compression as 1/2 inch.

engineering_analysis: The important reference is the sequence of contacts, not simply four launcher motors. Upstream acceleration reduces the velocity increment demanded of the drum, while the passive restraint prevents one contact from injecting fuel into an already occupied region. More powered surfaces can therefore lower useful flow. A retrofit also fixes the available path length and elevation; its compression distribution cannot safely be transplanted without the same incoming velocity and support geometry. Separately, the agitation priority hierarchy means collector deployment and automatic shooting agitation are competing commands rather than independent subsystems.

title: Dish packaging and shooting independence require a coordinated robot
construction: The interview describes an eleven-position dish, front and rear vertical roller sets to clear its center, approximately 425 degrees of turret freedom, a 3-inch main shooter wheel, a 1-inch upper roller and additional feed wheels. title: A rising fuel path makes agitation and service mass consequential
construction: The collector kicker changed from a hanging deployed bar to a member that folds with the hopper. Side agitation, passive dead-zone rollers, added gripping rollers and a belt-linked roller elevator feed the drum. An apparently small passive roller may be important because it removes a place where the moving stream can unload into a dead pocket. title: Protected carbon intake and continuous J-path launcher feed
construction: A 2×1 aluminum crash member protects a carbon intake roller. Later wrist plates use half-inch stock with raised hard-stop contact regions and pocketing. The shooter uses a J-shaped accelerating tunnel, a separate feeder, a four-X60 steel drum and powered hood rollers; its hood pivot is supported independently of the drum. title: Precondition fuel before a compact turret, then manage defended stability
construction: The interview describes eleven active carbon/silicone floor rollers powered by an X60 through a stated 2:1 reduction, with 3-mm-pitch GT2 inter-roller belts. A later acceleration stage is described as delivering approximately 8 m/s with near-zero incoming spin. Compact turret packaging shares shafts and places hood-drive hardware to limit diameter. A defended shooting mode cancels shooting on the move.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly cites efficiency at small pulley radii for its belt choice and compactness for the turret transmission layout. Its defended mode is explained as planting the robot to resist being pushed and emptying more accurately.
engineering_analysis: Preconditioning is a useful way to separate high-volume transport from precision release. A turret receiving fuel with controlled velocity and spin needs to add less correction, but it inherits errors in every upstream roller and transfer gap. The reported 8 m/s is an internal-stage claim, not a measured final trajectory specification or match-average rate. A planted mode also shows why turret capability does not require moving continuously: the best control mode depends on contact conditions. A future implementation must budget traction and battery demand for both upstream acceleration and chassis resistance.

title: Twin spindexers trade packaging freedom for multiple coupled interfaces
construction: The mechanism has two rotating floor/cone systems and uptake ramps, separately controlled kickers, independent turrets and hood adjustment. The interview describes X44-driven indexer systems, 6-inch aluminum flywheels replacing heavy steel trials, an under-mounted battery on a pinned removable panel, and chassis-speed-dependent intake voltage bounded around 6.5–12 V.

Fuel must be distributed to both cones, delivered through both ramps and accelerated without one path starving or overpacking. Moving-shot math must use the location of each turret rather than a single robot-center vector; angular chassis motion creates different local velocities at separated release points. title: Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness
construction: The interview distinguishes a former divided two-lane/double-spindexer arrangement from the drum rebuild with a roller floor. A powered lower intake roller was replaced by two 3/4-inch aluminum shafts with reduced compression. Compliant wheels near entry feed a J-shaped path; a guide was added after WPI wobble. title: Large inventory changes collector loading, frame clearance and drive gearing
construction: The interview reports approximately 115-fuel capacity, a 33.5×21.375-inch robot envelope before the described extension, a wide 3-inch two-X60 intake, a load shield above the collector, and hopper structure changed from angle to tube. A large stored column presses on its lowest contact surfaces, so a shield can be more valuable than another nominally faster roller. title: Surface contamination, inertia and power control interact
construction: The collector deploy angle was flattened after first-event jams. The retained interview account describes surgical tubing replaced by grippier floor surfaces after fuel debris caused slip. The shooter uses a four-X60 aluminum drum, powered upper rollers and a compact geared steel flywheel; transfer is sequenced after launcher speed is reached. A flywheel can smooth a transient without fixing an inadequate recharge rate or a hot motor. Robot logging should distinguish commanded voltage, actual bus voltage, current limit, speed error and fuel flow; otherwise starvation and electrical saturation can look like the same shooting symptom.

title: Passive feed solved one jam while rack durability remained unresolved
construction: The rack collector and belt floor feed an originally divided shooter that became one continuous drum. In the team’s later technical discussion, powered upper/lower indexing rollers overpacked the ramp; immobilizing the lower rollers corrected that feed issue. The static hood avoids an exposed powered-roller belt. The team separately reports repeated polycarbonate rack-tooth failures and a 45-A deploying/5-A deployed current-limit strategy at Worlds.
team_stated_reason: The stated priorities are simple, durable mechanisms and resistance to trench contact. The lower surface was made static to meter entry rather than forcing fuel into a congested ramp. The current-limit change aimed to let the intake collapse under impact; failures became less frequent but did not disappear.
engineering_analysis: This example needs two distinct failure histories. A feed-path change can be successful while the deployment structure remains unreliable. Stronger propulsion is not automatically the fix for a packing jam, and a high-performing alliance run does not certify rack durability. Source-reported storage also has a useful distinction: almost 70 geometric capacity versus commonly 50–60 in play. Protected interior PETG vector wheels surviving a season is not evidence that the same prints would survive as exposed intake wheels.
recommended_validation: Test the passive lower feed with full hopper pressure and varied fuel. Instrument deployment impact/current and inspect tooth-root damage. A proposed decoupling of intake sides is a future idea, not a fielded fix.

title: Trench access and speed-error feeding explain the rebuild
construction: A slotted three-roller transfer provides adjustable compression before a two-X60 high-inertia launcher. The flexible Hopper Flopper compresses under the trench and re-expands afterward. It can change autonomous arrival order and the opponent’s available supply. Speed-error-dependent feed is a form of demand management: slow entry when the launcher is behind instead of allowing a nominally high feed command to create low-energy misses. title: Capstan deployment and belt-floor lanes are dated fixes, not universal upgrades
construction: First-party replies describe 2-inch upper rollers, a 1.25-inch lower roller and about half an inch of compression. The robot changed from roller floor to belt floor between URI and UVM, and from rack deployment to a rope capstan after tooth damage. It reports lower current and faster feeding after the belt-floor change; belt spacing created lanes and reduced fuel spinning in place. Belt spacing can organize deformable fuel and remove an unproductive rotating contact state, but that result depends on piece size, belt spacing, load and friction. A capstan cannot skip discrete gear teeth, yet it can slip, stretch, lose tension or suffer anchor damage. The team’s prior capstan experience also changes development risk: the decision was supported by an existing implementation history rather than an untested mechanism adopted casually midseason.

construction: The interview describes four shoulder motors with a stated 111:1 reduction, a chain-driven dead-axis pivot, and a two-motor telescoping arm.
